a2Note: 68 PS as standard, but Kawasaki offers an official 35 kW restriction and markets the Ninja 650 in its A2 line-up in Europe.
beginnerNote: A friendly, predictable parallel twin with an upright riding position and an official A2 option, but the full 68 PS and sporty character reward a rider who has outgrown a 300–500cc machine.
whoFor: Riders who want everyday sportbike looks and weather protection with easygoing midrange grunt — a commuter on weekdays that still entertains on a Sunday mountain run.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you want genuine supersport performance or adjustable suspension — a ZX-6R or Ninja ZX-4RR crowd will find it soft.
about: The Ninja 650 pairs a 649cc parallel twin with a light trellis frame, giving a sporty-looking bike that is really a friendly all-rounder. The engine majors on low and midrange torque rather than top-end rush, and the riding position is far more upright than the full fairing suggests. Recent model years add traction control (KTRC) and a TFT dash with Bluetooth connectivity.
pros: Torquey, forgiving 649cc twin
Light handling and low 790 mm seat for a faired bike
Fairing gives real commuting weather protection
Official 35 kW A2 restriction available
TFT dash with smartphone connectivity and traction control
cons: Basic, largely non-adjustable suspension goes soft when pushed
No quickshifter even as an option on the base model
sources: Kawasaki UK specifications page for the 2026 Ninja 650 (kawasaki.co.uk)

a2Note: 68 PS as standard; an official Kawasaki 35 kW restriction kit makes it A2-legal, and Kawasaki markets an A2 version in Europe.
beginnerNote: Light, slim and unintimidating with a soft bottom-end and an assist/slipper clutch, though the full-power version still packs enough punch that it suits a second-season rider better than a day-one novice.
whoFor: Urban and B-road riders who want an agile, sharp-looking Sugomi naked with real-world torque, low running costs and an A2 pathway.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you regularly ride motorways or two-up — there is no wind protection and the pillion perch is small.
about: The Z650 is the naked sibling of the Ninja 650: the same 649cc parallel twin in a light trellis chassis with wide bars and aggressive Sugomi styling. At 188 kg with a 790 mm seat it is one of the most manageable middleweight nakeds, and the assist & slipper clutch keeps the lever action light. It trades outright power for punchy, accessible midrange.
pros: Agile, lightweight chassis with light clutch action
Punchy midrange from the proven 649cc twin
Low seat and slim waist suit shorter riders
Official 35 kW A2 restriction available
TFT dash with smartphone connectivity
cons: Zero wind protection for motorway work
Budget suspension is soft over hard riding

a2Note: 33.4 kW natively — fully A2-compliant with no restriction needed.
beginnerNote: One of the easiest first big bikes on sale: a 735 mm seat, 176 kg full of fuel, gentle throttle response and natively A2-legal power make it nearly foolproof while still being motorway-capable.
whoFor: New or returning riders and anyone short of inseam who wants a light, low, modern cruiser that is confidence-inspiring in town yet revs freely enough to hold its own out of it.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you want classic V-twin cruiser thump or plan long two-up touring — the parallel twin is smooth rather than characterful and the pillion pad is thin.
about: The Eliminator 500 revives Kawasaki's dragster-cruiser name around the 451cc parallel twin derived from the Ninja/Z 400 family, stroked for extra midrange. It blends a low-slung cruiser stance and 735 mm seat with sportbike-derived manners: light steering for an 18-inch front wheel, an eager top-end and modest 176 kg curb mass. LED lighting throughout and an optional SE trim round out a thoroughly modern take on the class.
pros: Very low 735 mm seat and light 176 kg curb weight
Natively A2-compliant 45 PS twin, no restrictor needed
Frugal 3.8 l/100km keeps range respectable from the 13 L tank
Easygoing riding position without extreme cruiser ergonomics
Modern LED lighting and gear-position-equipped LCD dash
cons: Limited rear suspension travel (90 mm) over rough roads
Small pillion pad and few touring amenities
Smooth twin lacks traditional cruiser character
sources: Kawasaki UK specifications page for the 2025 Eliminator 500 (kawasaki.co.uk)

a2Note: 62 kW is far above the 35 kW A2 limit and more than double it, so no A2 restriction is possible.
beginnerNote: Manageable power delivery and light clutch, but an 855 mm seat, 230 kg wet and a 21-inch front make it a lot of motorcycle for a first bike — better as a step up than a starting point.
whoFor: Adventure riders who genuinely intend to leave the tarmac: the 21-inch spoked front wheel, 220 mm of travel at both ends and a Gravel traction mode make it the most dirt-focused middleweight in Suzuki's range, while the 20 L tank and relaxed twin keep it an excellent road tourer.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you are short, ride mostly city streets, or want a light bike — the 855 mm seat and 230 kg are real obstacles, and the road-biased V-Strom 800 (cast wheels) is cheaper and lower.
about: The V-Strom 800DE is Suzuki's off-road-ready middleweight ADV, built around a 776cc 270-degree parallel twin with ride-by-wire, a bi-directional quickshifter and the S.I.R.S. electronics suite including a dedicated Gravel traction mode. Long-travel fully adjustable Showa suspension, 220 mm of ground clearance and wire-spoke 21/17-inch wheels set it apart from the street-focused V-Strom 800. It carries 20 litres of fuel and returns about 4.4 l/100km, giving genuine 400 km touring range.
pros: Real off-road ability: 21-inch spoked front, 220 mm travel and clearance
Flexible 776cc twin with standard two-way quickshifter
Comprehensive electronics incl. Gravel mode and switchable ABS
20 L tank plus ~4.4 l/100km economy for long range
Strong value against European rivals
cons: Tall 855 mm seat and 230 kg kerb weight intimidate shorter riders
No cruise control on the standard model
Block-pattern tyres and long suspension dull outright tarmac sharpness
